From the Time Domain to the Frequency Domain

Let’s look at the worksheet we started class with. The core idea is that the Fourier transform is a mathematical tool—a sort of wizard—that can convert a time domain signal (like a raw waveform) into a frequency domain spectrum.

If you record your voice, or the ringing of a wine glass, or the voltage output of a speaker, you are collecting a time-domain signal. We typically denote this signal as x(t), where the horizontal axis is time t.

When you feed this raw data into the Fourier transform algorithm, it spits out a new graph. On this new graph, the horizontal axis is no longer time; it is frequency f. We call this output the Fourier spectrum, denoted X(f). What this spectrum tells you is exactly what frequencies (or harmonics) are present in your original time-domain signal.

Spatial Periodicity: Beyond Just Time

While we often talk about signals oscillating in time, the Fourier transform is just as powerful for data that are periodic with position.

Think about an ocean wave frozen in a photograph, or the regular arrangement of atoms in a crystal lattice. If you feed an image of a crystal into a Fourier transform algorithm, it will quantify what spatial frequencies are present. In materials science and nanoscience, instead of talking about time-based frequency, we talk about wavelengths, or the d-spacing (the lattice parameter between atoms). Sometimes we use the inverse of the wavelength, known as the wave number or wave vector. This technique is heavily used alongside electron microscopy to analyze the periodic structures of nanomaterials. Any image that contains repeating, periodic patterns can be fed into this math to extract highly useful structural parameters.

If we take the Fourier transform of an electron microscopy image of a crystal lattice, what physical property does the resulting "frequency" actually represent?

Instead of a time-based frequency, the spatial frequency represents the inverse of the distance between repeating structures. In a crystal, this tells us the d-spacing or lattice parameter between the atoms!

The Simplest Case: A Pure Sinusoid

Let’s look at the simplest possible case: a pure sinusoidal wave. Suppose we have a signal that oscillates at a single, steady rate.

Here, we have a signal x(t) that repeats itself 3 times every second. We can write this mathematically as: \begin{equation} \tag{1} x(t) = \cos(2\pi \cdot 3t) = \sum_{n=1}^{1} A_n \cos(2\pi f_n t) \end{equation} where the amplitude A_1 = 1 and the frequency f_1 = 3 \text{ Hz}.

If we take the Fourier transform of this signal, what should we expect? Since there is only one frequency present, our mathematical wizard should just give us a single, sharp spike at 3 Hz.

And that is exactly what we get! One frequency in the time domain equals one spike in the frequency domain.

Now, you might be thinking, “Coach, I didn’t need a fancy algorithm to tell me that.” And you would be right! If you have a pure sinusoid, you can just look at the graph, measure the period T (which is 1/3 of a second here), and calculate the frequency as f = 1/T = 3 \text{ Hz}.

For example, on your recent quiz extra credit, you looked at an oscilloscope trace of a pure sinusoidal signal. You saw that one full period spanned 2.5 divisions at 2 \text{ ms} per division, giving a period of T = 5 \text{ ms} = 5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}. Taking the inverse, the frequency is: \begin{equation} f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}} = 200 \text{ Hz} \tag{2} \end{equation} Because the signal was a pure sine wave, its Fourier transform is just a single, sharp vertical line at 200 \text{ Hz}. Alternatively, you could use a Python script to curve-fit the data to a model like x(t) = A \sin(2\pi f t).

But what if your data is messy? What if it is complicated? That is where the Fourier transform becomes incredibly powerful.

Uncovering Hidden Harmonics

Let’s look at a more complicated waveform.

If you just stare at this time-domain signal, it is lumpy and irregular. It is not obvious how many frequencies are hiding in there. Good luck curve-fitting this if you don’t know what you are looking for! But if we break it down, this signal is actually the sum of two pure harmonics: \begin{equation} \tag{3} x(t) = \cos(2\pi \cdot 2t) + \cos(2\pi \cdot 5t) = \sum_{n=1}^{2} A_n \cos(2\pi f_n t) \end{equation} where the amplitudes are equal (A_1 = A_2 = 1), and the frequencies are f_1 = 2 \text{ Hz} and f_2 = 5 \text{ Hz}.

When we feed this lumpy signal into the Fourier transform, the wizard easily separates them out.

We get exactly two spikes: one at 2 Hz and one at 5 Hz.

What if the two components do not have the same strength?

Here, the 5 Hz component is noticeably smaller. The mathematical representation is: \begin{equation} \tag{4} x(t) = \cos(2\pi \cdot 2t) + 0.35\cos(2\pi \cdot 5t) = \sum_{n=1}^{2} A_n \cos(2\pi f_n t) \end{equation} where A_1 = 1 and A_2 = 0.35. The Fourier transform does not just tell us which frequencies are present; it also tells us their relative amplitudes.

The height of the spike in the frequency spectrum |X(f)| corresponds directly to the amplitude of that harmonic in the time domain. The 5 Hz spike is exactly 35% the height of the 2 Hz spike.

The Missing Piece: Phase Shift

Now, let’s revisit a question from your homework: If I have the Fourier spectrum of your voice, can I exactly reproduce your voice using a sound-producing robot?

Most of you guessed no, and you are correct! But why? If we know exactly how much of each frequency is present, shouldn’t we be able to just add them all up and get the exact same waveform back?

The catch is phase. The magnitude of the Fourier spectrum |X(f)| tells us the amplitudes of the frequencies, but it tells us nothing about how those different harmonics stack up against each other in time. This relative shift in time is called the phase shift.

Let’s see what happens to our two-frequency signal if we flip the phase of the 5 Hz component.

We add a phase shift of \pi to the 5 Hz term: \begin{equation} \tag{5} x(t) = \cos(2\pi \cdot 2t) + 0.35\cos(2\pi \cdot 5t + \pi) = \sum_{n=1}^{2} A_n \cos(2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n) \end{equation} where \varphi_1 = 0 and \varphi_2 = \pi.

Look at the time-domain signal (the solid teal line). It has an entirely different shape compared to the previous example (shown as the dashed line)! The peaks and valleys stack up differently. If this were a sound wave, it would sound different to your ear.

But what happens when we take the Fourier transform?

The spectrum |X(f)| looks exactly the same as before! We still have a spike at 2 Hz and a smaller spike at 5 Hz. The Fourier transform algorithm (at least, the magnitude part of it that we plot here) throws away the phase information. Because of this, you cannot reconstruct a complex waveform just from its amplitude spectrum.

If two sound waves have the exact same amplitude spectrum |X(f)|, why might they still sound different to your ear?

The amplitude spectrum only tells us how much of each frequency is present, but it throws away the phase information. Phase tells us how those different harmonic waves are shifted in time relative to one another. If the peaks and valleys stack up differently, the resulting combined waveform changes shape, which alters the sound.

Building Any Shape: Fourier Series

Things get really fun when we add even more frequencies.

Here is a funky waveform made of five different frequency components: \begin{equation} \tag{6} x(t) = \cos(2\pi t) + 0.8\cos(2\pi \cdot 2t) + \dots + 0.3\cos(2\pi \cdot 5t) = \sum_{n=1}^{5} A_n \cos(2\pi n t) \end{equation}

The Fourier transform reveals all five spikes, beautifully lined up. This leads us to a profound mathematical truth: Any periodic function, no matter how complicated, squarish, or triangular it looks, can be exactly replicated by adding up enough sinusoidal terms with different frequencies, amplitudes, and phases. This infinite sum is called a Fourier series.

Let’s look at a square wave.

A square wave has very sharp, abrupt changes. To build this out of smooth, round sine waves, we have to add up an infinite number of harmonics! \begin{equation} \tag{7} x(t) = \frac{4}{\pi} \left[ \sin(2\pi t) + \frac{1}{3}\sin(2\pi \cdot 3t) + \frac{1}{5}\sin(2\pi \cdot 5t) + \dots \right] = \frac{4}{\pi} \sum_{n=1,3,5,\dots}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n} \sin(2\pi n t) \end{equation} We start with a fundamental frequency (1 Hz), and then add odd harmonics (3 Hz, 5 Hz, 7 Hz, etc.) with decreasing amplitudes.

When we take the Fourier transform of a square wave, we get a series of spikes at the odd integers, with their heights dropping off proportionally to 1/n.

Non-Periodic Signals and the Middle Finger

So far, we have only looked at periodic signals—things that repeat forever. What if a signal just happens once and stops?

Here we have a single, rectangular pulse. It is not periodic; you can think of its period as being infinitely long (T \to \infty). Because the period is infinite, the spacing between the harmonics (1/T) shrinks to zero. \begin{equation} \tag{8} x(t) = \lim_{\Delta f \to 0} \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} X(f_n)\cos(2\pi f_n t) \Delta f = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(f)\cos(2\pi f t) df \end{equation} Instead of discrete spikes, the spectrum becomes a continuous function: \begin{equation} \tag{9} X(f) = \frac{\sin(\pi f \tau)}{\pi f} \end{equation} where the pulse width is \tau = 0.5 \text{ s}.

Finally, let’s take this to the extreme limit. What if we make our pulse infinitely narrow?

This is called a delta function, \delta(t). It is a single, infinitely sharp spike at t=0. \begin{equation} \tag{10} x(t) = \delta(t) = \lim_{\Delta f \to 0} \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \cos(2\pi f_n t) \Delta f = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \cos(2\pi f t) df \end{equation} If you take the Fourier transform of this infinitely narrow pulse, what do you get? \begin{equation} \tag{11} X(f) = 1 \end{equation} You get a flat, horizontal line! An infinitely sharp pulse in the time domain contains every single frequency in equal amounts.

If you wanted to test a speaker’s ability to play every single audio frequency at the exact same volume, what kind of time-domain signal should you send into it?

You would send an infinitely narrow, sharp pulse, also known as a delta function. As we just saw, the Fourier transform of a delta function is a flat horizontal line in the frequency domain. This means it contains all frequencies in equal amounts, making it a great theoretical tool for testing the full frequency response of a system.

This brings me to a borderline inappropriate joke I learned in grad school. When you are driving and someone is very aggressive, you might feel the urge to give them the middle finger. I don’t recommend doing that. But here is a nerdy alternative: you can hold up a flat hand (representing a flat line) and mutter, “Take a Fourier transform of this!” Because the Fourier transform of a flat line is a single, sharp spike—a middle finger. And conversely, as we just saw, the Fourier transform of a middle finger (a delta function) is a flat line.
